title: Languages, Compilers & Runtimes
summary: Your code is just text until something translates it into actions a CPU can do. Knowing that path is what separates "I can code" from "I know what my code costs."

blocks.markdown:
A CPU only understands machine code; everything else is a translation layer to get there.

- A **compiler** translates source to a lower-level form **without running it**, producing a separate artifact.
- An **interpreter** executes your code directly, translating-and-doing as it goes.
- The **AST** (Abstract Syntax Tree) is your code as a tree of operations — the central object everything after parsing works on.
- A **runtime** is the machinery that supports the running program: stack, heap, calling convention.

blocks.subTitle: Which strategy when
blocks.markdown:
Pick the execution strategy by what you optimize for.

| If you want | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Fast startup, small binaries | AOT (Rust, Go, C++) |
| Peak throughput on servers | JIT (JVM, V8, .NET) |
| Fast iteration / glue | Interpreter (Python, Ruby) |
| One artifact, many OSes | Bytecode VM (JVM, CLR) |

blocks.subTitle: The pipeline
blocks.markdown:
A compiler is an assembly line; each stage hands the next a cleaner structure.

![Compiler pipeline from source to machine code](assets/languages-compilers-runtimes/compiler-pipeline.svg)

- **Lex** — split the raw string into tokens (the words).
- **Parse** — build the AST, capturing nesting and precedence.
- **Semantic check** — declarations, types, scope, via a symbol table.
- **IR** — lower to a language- and CPU-neutral middle form.
- **Optimize** — passes rewrite the IR to run faster or smaller.
- **Code gen** — emit machine code for one specific CPU.

assets.alt: Compiler pipeline from source to machine code

blocks.subTitle: The AST
blocks.markdown:
The AST encodes structure a flat token stream can't.

![AST for the expression 2 + 3 * 4](assets/languages-compilers-runtimes/ast-expression.svg)

- `2 + 3 * 4` becomes a tree with `+` at the root and the `*` subtree below it.
- Because `*` sits **deeper**, evaluating bottom-up computes `3 * 4` first — precedence lives in the shape, no parentheses needed.
- "Abstract" means it drops noise like semicolons and parens once they've done their job.
- Type checking, optimization, and code gen all walk this tree.

blocks.subTitle: Why an IR
blocks.markdown:
The intermediate representation decouples the front end from the back end.

- With **M** source languages and **N** target CPUs, direct compilers cost `M × N`.
- A shared IR needs only `M` front ends plus `N` back ends — `M + N`.
- It's also the right level to run portable optimizations **once**, not per language and chip.
- LLVM IR is the canonical example, shared by Clang, `rustc`, and Swift.

blocks.subTitle: Interpreter vs AOT vs JIT
blocks.markdown:
Execution strategy is just how far down the pipeline you go before running, and when.

![Interpreter versus AOT versus JIT execution paths](assets/languages-compilers-runtimes/exec-paths.svg)

- **Interpreter** — stops early and walks the AST or bytecode, executing each node. No native code.
- **AOT** — runs the full pipeline to machine code before shipping; running is just executing the binary.
- **JIT** — interprets first for fast startup, then a profiler finds hot code and compiles only that to native at runtime.

assets.alt: Interpreter versus AOT versus JIT execution paths

blocks.subTitle: Stack, heap, calling convention
blocks.markdown:
The runtime is the machinery supporting your program while it runs.

- **Call stack** — per-call frames holding arguments, locals, and the return address. Pushed on call, popped on return. Cheap, but data dies when the function returns.
- **Heap** — for data that outlives its creator or whose size is unknown at compile time. Slower, and someone must reclaim it (manual, GC, or ownership).
- **Calling convention** — the contract for which args go in which registers, who cleans up, and where the return value lands. Must be standard so separately-compiled code interoperates.

blocks.subTitle: Bytecode & the VM
blocks.markdown:
Many languages compile not to native code but to **bytecode** for an imaginary stack-based VM.

```text
2 + 3   compiles to:
PUSH 2
PUSH 3
ADD       # pops two, pushes their sum
```

- A stack VM has no registers; instructions push and pop an operand stack.
- The VM (JVM, CPython, .NET CLR) is a program that runs these instructions.
- Bytecode is portable (one `.class` runs on any JVM), compact, and an ideal input for a JIT.

blocks.subTitle: Why a JIT can beat AOT
blocks.markdown:
An AOT compiler compiles once, blind; a JIT measures the actual run.

- **De-virtualize** — if a polymorphic call only ever hits one type, inline it behind a cheap guard.
- **Optimize the hot branch** — lay out the common path straight-line for the branch predictor.
- **Recompile if wrong** — when a speculation fails, **deoptimize** to the interpreter, then recompile.
- **The cost is warmup** — early code runs interpreted and slow, and compiling burns CPU and memory.

blocks.subTitle: Picking a strategy
blocks.markdown:
Match the runtime to what dominates your job.

- **Startup or predictable latency dominates** (CLIs, serverless, trading) → AOT native. No warmup, no JIT pauses.
- **Long-lived heavy server** → JIT; warmup amortizes away and adaptive optimization wins on throughput.
- **Iteration and glue matter most** → an interpreter is fine until profiling says otherwise.
- **Correctness on a large team** → static, strong typing turns the compiler into a free reviewer.

blocks.subTitle: Typing axes
blocks.markdown:
Static-vs-dynamic and strong-vs-weak are **independent** axes.

| Axis | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Static vs dynamic | When types are checked: compile time or runtime |
| Strong vs weak | How much it resists implicit conversions |

- Python is **dynamic but strong** (`"3" + 5` errors); C is **static but weak** (cast almost anything).
- **Type inference** lets the compiler deduce unwritten types: `var x = 41 + 1` infers `int`.

blocks.subTitle: Real runtimes
blocks.markdown:
The famous runtimes are variations on interpret-then-compile-the-hot-parts.

- **HotSpot JVM** — interprets bytecode first, then C1 (light) and C2 (aggressive) JIT-compile hot methods; deoptimizes when a guess fails.
- **V8** — Ignition interpreter plus TurboFan JIT; **hidden classes** track object shapes so it can specialize for the types actually flowing through.
- **Go** — deliberate pure **AOT**, no VM; bundles a tiny runtime into one static binary for fast startup.
- **LLVM** — the `M + N` idea shipped: many front ends emit IR, one optimizer and back end serve all.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Compiled is always faster than interpreted."** A warmed-up JIT can match C; a bad algorithm in C loses to a good one in Python.
- **"The AST is the machine code."** It's an early, CPU-agnostic tree — IR, optimization, and code gen still lie between.
- **"Strong typing means static typing."** Different axes: strong/weak is about conversions, static/dynamic is about *when* checks happen.
- **"Stack and heap are data structures."** Here they're **memory regions** — unrelated to the heap from [heaps-priority-queues](heaps-priority-queues).
- **"GC means I never think about memory."** Allocation rate and pauses drive tail latency.
